content:
1	Thank you, Senator Markey and Senator Warren for having me this morning.
     2	 My name is Ellana Stinson. I am a board-certified emergency medicine physician and have
     3	 practiced emergency medicine for 15 years.
     4	 From 2013 to 2020, I worked on staff as an emergency medicine physician at Carney Hospital,
     5	 Good Samaritan and the former Quincy Hospital, all part of the Steward Health System. In
     6	 addition, over the past 11 years, I have worked intermittently throughout the country at various
     7	 facilities run and operated by HCA, Envision, Tenant, Team Health and CHS.
     8	 When I entered medicine, I deeply loved what I did. Caring for patients in their most vulnerable
     9	 moments and working in beautifully orchestrated chaos while bearing witness to so many life
    10	 changing moments filled me with pride at the end of each shift. Unfortunately, so much of what
    11	 I loved about Emergency Medicine has changed drastically over the years.
    12	 Initially, my time at Carney felt very fresh and fulfilling. Being able to serve a very diverse
    13	 population in the Dorchester neighborhood of Boston was essentially how I always imagined my
    14	 career trajectory, serving the most vulnerable populations. But when I could no longer care for
    15	 my patients the way I would want a loved one treated, I had to make decisions to stay or
    16	 go. Having spent time at several other Stewart facilities briefly, I began to realize how resources
    17	 were being dwindled down and pulled from each facility. Most of the facilities no longer had
    18	 certain speciality services and Quincy Hospital, eventually was taken down to bare bones before
    19	 its ultimate closure. Not having blood products, respiratory therapy at times or certain specialty
    20	 services no longer felt like I was able to provide safe or quality care. What is happening here in
    21	 the Commonwealth is happening around the country.
    22	 We have now seen the buyouts, mergers and acquisitions led by private equity firms of over 30%
    23	 of hospitals in the US. Having spent time at other PE sites around the country the level of
    24	 deprivation was seemingly worse in some areas. Increased wait times and critical shortage of
    25	 staff leading to dangerous boarding levels and critically dangerous patient to nurse ratios in the
    26	 emergency department, seeing upwards to 14 to 1 ratios at times. All of this only to be
    27	 exacerbated by the pandemic which resulted in increased cost of care, infection rates, mortality
    28	 and even death.
    29	 Practicing medicine in many PE led places is no longer about patient safety and quality, but
    30	 about making medical decisions and judgment due corporate decision making with profit
    31	 motives at the expense of patients. Forcing staff to see patients in the waiting room in order to
    32	 have it appear wait times were being reduced and improving door to doc times, calling codes for
    33	 sepsis and strokes in order to find innovative ways to make profits. Increasingly daunting
    34	 metrics required of physicians and other staff to meet were nearly unattainable and unsafe in
    35	 many instances, but very much expected. In addition, many sites across the country began to
    36	 remove emergency physicians from in-network, resulting in higher bills for patients known as
    37	 surprise billing. These profit gaining practices not only harm patients but also increase financial
    38	 burdens on patients who do not have a choice of where they will go when they are experiencing
    39	 crushing chest pain or stroke-like symptoms. Especially when the next closest facility has been
    40	 in some of my experiences, upwards to an hour away.
    41	 Most of the facilities I worked in were in very vulnerable populations that were mostly people of
    42	 color, low income, or had limited access to other facilities or primary care services. Forcing
    43	 them to only seek their care at a PE backed site. It is also known that most of the buyouts are of
    44	 hospitals and facilities already struggling or with higher Medicaid and Medicare populations
    45	 which ultimately affects our most vulnerable populations. It is critical we consider not only the
    46	 impact these facilities have on our health care system, but also on the worsening care access and
    47	 quality being provided to those communities already harmed by historical injury. The
    48	 financialization of medicine will continue to exacerbate health disparities despite work being
    49	 done on the ground to close these gaps.
    50	 In addition, these Private Equity backed facilities are where I typically run into other emergency
    51	 physicians of color. As it pertains to myself and my colleagues, these practices often felt unsafe,
    52	 which sparked many questions of medical legal risk as well as the emotional toll it takes on all of
    53	 us who enter this profession to do no harm. In addition, being on staff at a PE backed facility
    54	 also would not qualify physicians swimming in student debt for loan forgiveness. A profession
    55	 once competitive when I first began my medical journey is now one of the least competitive
    56	 fields to enter as students bear witness to the destruction of the profession. In 2023, 554 of the
    57	 residency spots went unfilled. We also saw more PE backed hospitals opening residency
    58	 programs that were not adequately equipped to provide the proper training for an emergency
    59	 medicine trainee.
    60	 We train to deal with hard stuff, but we are running out of options on how to continue providing
    61	safe and adequate care at these PE run facilities.

Based on `doc.txt`, here is a summary of Ellana's background and her concerns:

**Ellana's Background in Medicine**
- Her name is Ellana Stinson, and she is a board-certified emergency medicine physician with 15 years of practice in emergency medicine.
- From 2013 to 2020, she worked on staff as an emergency medicine physician at Carney Hospital, Good Samaritan, and the former Quincy Hospital, all part of the Steward Health System.
- Over the past 11 years, she has also worked intermittently throughout the country at various facilities run by HCA, Envision, Tenant, Team Health, and CHS.
- When she entered medicine, she deeply loved the work—caring for patients in their most vulnerable moments and working in "beautifully orchestrated chaos" filled her with pride.

**Her Concerns About Changes in Emergency Medicine**
- **Resource depletion:** At Steward facilities, resources were dwindled and pulled from each facility; many lost specialty services, and Quincy Hospital was reduced to "bare bones" before closure. The absence of blood products, respiratory therapy, and certain specialty services made her feel she could no longer provide safe or quality care.
- **Private equity buyouts:** Over 30% of US hospitals have been bought by private equity firms, and at PE sites she worked at, the level of deprivation was sometimes worse.
- **Staffing and safety problems:** Increased wait times, critical staff shortages, dangerous boarding levels, and critically dangerous patient-to-nurse ratios in the ED—up to 14-to-1 at times—were exacerbated by the pandemic, which increased the cost of care, infection rates, and mortality.
- **Profit over patient care:** At PE-led places, medicine is no longer about patient safety and quality but about corporate decision-making with profit motives. Examples include forcing staff to see patients in the waiting room to make wait times appear reduced, and calling codes for sepsis and strokes to find ways to make profits.
- **Unattainable metrics:** Increasingly daunting metrics required of physicians and staff were nearly unattainable and unsafe in many instances, yet expected.
- **Surprise billing:** Many sites removed emergency physicians from in-network, resulting in higher bills for patients (surprise billing), which harms patients and increases financial burdens on people with no choice of where to go during emergencies—especially when the next closest facility can be an hour away.
- **Impact on vulnerable populations:** Most facilities she worked in served vulnerable populations—mostly people of color, low-income, or with limited access to other facilities or primary care—forcing them to seek care only at PE-backed sites. Most buyouts target already-struggling hospitals with higher Medicaid and Medicare populations, worsening care access and quality in communities already harmed by historical injury, and exacerbating health disparities.
- **Toll on physicians:** These practices felt unsafe to her and her colleagues (many emergency physicians of color), raising questions of medical-legal risk and the emotional toll on those who entered the profession to do no harm. Being on staff at a PE-backed facility also did not qualify physicians with student debt for loan forgiveness.
- **Decline of the profession:** A profession once competitive when she began is now one of the least competitive fields to enter, as students witness its destruction. In 2023, 554 residency spots went unfilled, and more PE-backed hospitals opened residency programs not adequately equipped to properly train emergency medicine trainees.
- She concludes that while they train to deal with hard situations, they are running out of options for continuing to provide safe and adequate care at PE-run facilities.
